The current marker is INTERVIEW-10-c7af58f8f0ddde26. The screen shows Palindrome Partitioning II: solve(s) must return the minimum cuts that partition a nonempty string into palindromes, with no stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Use dynamic programming, processing substring endpoints from left to right. Record whether s[start..end] is a palindrome: its endpoints must match, and either its length is at most two or its interior is already a palindrome. For each prefix ending at end, start with end cuts—the single-character partition—and consider every palindromic suffix: use zero cuts if start is zero, otherwise cuts[start − 1] + 1.

The invariant is that after processing end, cuts[end] is the minimum for that prefix, and all palindrome entries ending there are correct. Earlier endpoints supply the interior checks and optimal earlier partitions. Every valid partition has a final palindromic suffix, so considering all such suffixes finds the optimum. Return the minimum for the full string; time and space are both O(n²).

Boundary cases: one character or an entirely palindromic string needs zero cuts; two unequal characters need one; a string with no longer palindromes needs n − 1. The example "aab" needs one cut, "aa|b". Empty input is outside the stated contract. No implementation yet.

Marker: INTERVIEW-11-700ea78ef836ec52.

Use a monotonic deque of indices for solve(nums, k). For each index, remove expired indices from the front, remove indices with smaller or equal values from the back, then append the current index. Once a full window exists, append the front value to the result.

Invariant: indices increase from front to back, all belong to the current window, and their values strictly decrease. The front therefore holds the maximum. Removing a smaller or equal earlier value is safe because the newer value is at least as large and expires later.

Boundary cases: k = 1 returns every element; k = nums.length returns one overall maximum; a single-element input returns that element. Duplicate maxima, negative numbers, and increasing or decreasing inputs all work. The contract guarantees 1 <= k <= nums.length, so empty inputs and invalid k are outside scope.

Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once: O(n) time, O(k) auxiliary space, plus O(n − k + 1) output space. In JavaScript, use constant-time deque operations rather than Array.shift().

Use interval dynamic programming: pad nums with a 1 at each end, and choose each balloon as the last one burst inside an interval. If k is last between boundaries left and right, the candidate score is dp[left][k] + dp[k][right] + values[left] * values[k] * values[right]. Take the maximum over all interior k.

Invariant: dp[left][right] is the maximum coins from bursting every balloon strictly between those boundaries while keeping the boundaries intact. Process intervals from shortest to longest so both smaller subproblems are ready; choosing the last balloon makes its surviving neighbors exactly the two boundaries.

Boundary cases: an interval with no interior balloons earns 0; an empty input therefore returns 0, and a single balloon returns its value. Zero-valued balloons need no special handling. The attachment does not specify value constraints: if negatives are allowed, initialize nonempty interval maxima to negative infinity, not zero, because every balloon must be burst.

The final answer is the interval between the two added 1s. Time is O(n³), and space is O(n²).

Use coordinate compression: numerically sort the distinct values and assign ascending ranks starting at 1. Scan right to left, querying a Fenwick tree through rank − 1 to get each answer, then insert the current rank. This takes O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Invariant: before processing index i, the tree contains exactly the frequencies of nums[i + 1..n − 1]. Compression preserves ordering, and querying below the current rank excludes equal values; inserting afterward maintains the invariant.

Boundary cases: an empty array returns []; a singleton returns [0]; equal values and increasing arrays produce all zeros; a strictly decreasing array produces [n − 1, n − 2, ..., 0]. Negative values work unchanged through compression, and the smallest rank queries an empty prefix, returning zero. The contract requires no stdin/stdout, imports, or exports; no implementation yet.

Use memoized depth-first search. From each cell, explore only strictly larger neighbors above, below, left, and right. Its longest path is 1 plus the maximum neighbor result, or 1 if no larger neighbor exists; return the maximum over all cells.

Invariant: each completed memo entry is the exact longest increasing path starting at that cell. Strict increases prevent cycles, and caching ensures each cell is computed once. Time and auxiliary space are O(rows × columns), including the recursion stack.

The supplied example returns 4 via 1 → 2 → 6 → 9. Empty-matrix behavior is unspecified in TASK.md; returning 0 would be a reasonable convention if empty input is allowed. Very long paths can exceed JavaScript’s recursion limit, so an iterative topological approach is safer if large matrices are expected.

Use modified merge sort to count pairs i < j where nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]. Recursively count pairs within each half, then count cross-half pairs before merging. For each left-half value in ascending order, advance a pointer through the sorted right half while the strict inequality holds; the number of passed right-half values is its contribution.

Invariant: each recursive call returns the exact pair count for its original index range and leaves that range sorted. Every left-half index originally precedes every right-half index, and the counting pointer never moves backward because increasing the left value cannot invalidate an already qualifying right value. Merge with a separate pointer pass; ordinary merge comparisons do not establish the doubled-value condition.

Duplicates can count when negative: [-1, -1] returns 1 because -1 > -2, whereas [2, 1] returns 0. Numeric limits are not specified; exact integer comparisons require values and their doubles to remain safely representable in JavaScript.

Time: O(n log n). Auxiliary space: O(n).
